title: CDL basics: classes, endorsements and your permit
summary: Which license class you need, what endorsements are, and the steps from permit to CDL.
body: A commercial driver's license (CDL) comes in three classes, based on the vehicle. Class A covers combinations, like a tractor-trailer, with a gross combination weight rating of 26,001 pounds or more, where the towed unit is over 10,000 pounds. Class B covers heavy single vehicles over 26,000 pounds, like dump trucks and box trucks, towing 10,000 pounds or less. Class C covers smaller vehicles that carry 16 or more people (counting the driver) or placarded hazardous materials.

Endorsements are add-ons for special vehicles or cargo. Each one has its own knowledge test: H for hazardous materials, N for tank vehicles, T for doubles and triples, P for passenger vehicles, and S for school buses. X is a combined tanker and hazmat endorsement.

Your first step is the commercial learner's permit (CLP). You'll need a DOT medical card from a certified examiner, then you pass the knowledge tests at your state's licensing office. Everyone takes General Knowledge. Most drivers also take Air Brakes, and Class A drivers take Combination Vehicles.

Once you have the permit, you must hold it at least 14 days before the skills test. You can drive for practice only with a qualified CDL holder in the front seat beside you. Before the skills test, first-time Class A and B drivers must also finish Entry-Level Driver Training (ELDT) from a provider on the FMCSA's registry. For Hazmat, the ELDT theory must be done before you take the hazmat knowledge test.

title: Vehicle inspection
summary: How to inspect a truck before, during and after a trip, and what makes it unsafe.
body: Inspections catch problems before they cause a breakdown or a crash, and inspectors can put an unsafe vehicle out of service. You'll inspect before every trip, check things during the trip, and report problems at the end of the day.

Most drivers follow the seven-step method. It starts with a vehicle overview: walk up and look for damage, fluid leaks, leaning and anything in the way. Then check the engine compartment, start the engine and check the gauges and controls inside the cab, turn off the engine and check the lights, do a full walk-around, check the signal lights, and finish with a brake check.

Know the out-of-service limits. Steering tires need at least 4/32 inch of tread and other tires 2/32 inch. Steering wheel play over 10 degrees (about 2 inches on a 20-inch wheel) is too much. A leaf spring missing a quarter or more of its leaves is out of service. Never mix radial and bias-ply tires on the same axle, and recapped tires aren't allowed on the front wheels of a bus.

Watch for small clues. Rust trails around lug nuts can mean the nuts are loose. Exhaust leaks can let carbon monoxide into the cab. Cuts that show the tire's cord, bulges, and leaks all make a tire unsafe.

title: Basic control: steering, shifting and backing
summary: How to steer, shift and back a big vehicle safely.
body: Hold the wheel firmly with both hands on opposite sides. If you hit a curb or pothole, the wheel can jerk out of a loose grip.

Many trucks have manual transmissions that need double clutching: press the clutch and shift to neutral, release the clutch, let the engine speed match the next gear, then press the clutch again and shift. Shift down before hills and curves, not in the middle of them.

Backing is one of the riskiest things you'll do, because you can't see everything behind you. Avoid it when you can. When you must back, get out and look first, back slowly, use your mirrors on both sides, and use a helper. Back toward the driver's side whenever possible, so you can see the rear of the vehicle out your window.

Turns take planning. For a right turn, go straight until the rear clears the corner, then turn, keeping the back of the vehicle close to the curb so cars can't slip in beside you. For a left turn, reach the center of the intersection before you turn. If there are two left-turn lanes, use the right-hand one.

title: Seeing, signaling and stopped vehicles
summary: How to scan, use mirrors, signal your moves and warn traffic when you're stopped.
body: Look 12 to 15 seconds ahead. At highway speed that's about a quarter mile, enough time to spot trouble and slow down or change lanes smoothly. Check your mirrors regularly and before every lane change, turn or merge.

Know your mirrors. Convex (curved) mirrors show a wider area, but they make things look smaller and farther away than they really are. Large trucks have big blind spots directly behind and along the right side, and close in front and beside the cab.
Signal early and clearly so other drivers know what you're doing. Don't wave other drivers to pass you; if they crash, you could be blamed.

If you stop on the road or shoulder, turn on your four-way flashers right away and set out warning triangles within 10 minutes. On a two-lane road, put one about 10 feet from the vehicle on the traffic side, one about 100 feet behind and one about 100 feet ahead. On a divided or one-way road, put all three behind you at about 10, 100 and 200 feet. Behind a hill or curve, move the rear one back as far as 500 feet.

title: Speed, stopping distance and space
summary: Why trucks need so much room to stop, and how to keep a safe cushion around you.
body: Total stopping distance has three parts: perception distance (the time to see a hazard and recognize it), reaction distance (an alert driver needs about three-quarters of a second to react), and braking distance. A loaded truck at highway speed needs more than a football field to stop.

Speed matters more than most people think. Double your speed and your braking distance grows about four times. Weight matters too, but not how you'd expect: an empty truck can take longer to stop, because brakes, tires and springs are built for heavy loads and an empty truck has less traction.

Keep at least one second of following distance for every 10 feet of vehicle length at speeds under 40 mph. Above 40 mph, add one more second. A 40-foot truck needs 4 seconds below 40 mph and 5 seconds above it. Count the seconds after the vehicle ahead passes a fixed point.
If someone tailgates you, don't speed up or brake-check them. Open up more space in front of you so you can slow down gradually, and let them pass.

title: Night, weather and mountain driving
summary: How to handle darkness, rain, ice, fog, heat and long downgrades.
body: At night, drive slowly enough to stop within the area your headlights show. Switch to low beams within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle and when you're following someone.

Wet roads cut your traction, and with enough water your tires can hydroplane at speeds as low as 30 mph. In winter, black ice is the hidden danger: it's so thin the road just looks wet. If ice is forming on your mirrors or antenna, the road is probably icing too. Turn off your retarder on wet, icy or snowy roads. In fog, slow down and use low beams and fog lights; high beams reflect back and blind you.
Heat is hard on tires. In hot weather, check them every 2 hours or 100 miles.

On long downgrades, gravity is working against your brakes. Pick a low gear before you start down, since shifting on a steep grade can be hard or impossible. Then use snub braking: when you reach 5 mph over your safe speed, brake firmly until you're 5 mph under it, then release. If your safe speed is 40 mph, brake at 45 and release at 35. Riding the brakes overheats them and causes brake fade. If your brakes fail, use an escape ramp.

title: Skids, emergencies, fires and crashes
summary: How to avoid a crash, recover from a skid and handle fires and accident scenes.
body: Most serious skids come from driving too fast for conditions. Over-braking, over-steering and over-accelerating cause them too. If your drive wheels skid, take your foot off the accelerator and stop braking so the wheels can roll again, then steer where you want to go and be ready to countersteer.

In an emergency, steering is often faster than stopping. If you need to swerve, steering right is usually safest, since it keeps you out of oncoming traffic. If you have to leave the road, avoid hard braking until you've slowed to about 20 mph, and keep one set of wheels on the pavement if you can. With ABS, brake firmly and let the system keep the wheels from locking. Without ABS, use controlled or stab braking.

If your vehicle catches fire, get off the road and park in an open area away from buildings, trees and other vehicles. Never pull into a service station. Stay upwind while you fight the fire. Class B extinguishers are for flammable liquids and Class C for electrical fires.

At a crash, first protect the area with your flashers and triangles so it doesn't get worse. Then call for help and care for the injured. Don't move a seriously hurt person unless there's danger, like a fire.

title: Railroad crossings, alcohol, drugs and fatigue
summary: Crossing tracks safely and staying fit to drive.
body: Trains can't stop quickly; a freight train can need a mile or more. Never try to beat a train. Pick a gear that gets you all the way across before you start, and never shift gears on the tracks. Make sure there's room on the other side for your whole vehicle, and watch out for raised crossings, where low trailers can get stuck.

Commercial drivers are held to a stricter alcohol limit: 0.04%, half the usual limit for car drivers. Any detectable amount below that still puts you out of service for 24 hours. A first DUI in a commercial vehicle means losing your CDL for at least a year. Only time sobers you up; coffee and cold showers don't.
Fatigue causes crashes too. The only cure is sleep. If you start drifting or yawning, pull over somewhere safe and rest.
Phones are a big distraction. Federal rules ban texting and holding a phone while driving a commercial vehicle. Hands-free use only, and keep it short.

title: Cargo: weight, securement and inspection
summary: How to load, secure and check cargo, even when someone else loaded it.
body: You're responsible for your cargo, even if someone else loaded it. That means making sure it's secured and within weight limits, and checking it as you go.

GVWR is the maximum loaded weight a single vehicle is rated for. Overloading makes braking and steering worse and is illegal. Even with a sealed load you can't inspect, you're still responsible for staying within gross and axle weight limits.

Keep heavy cargo low. Stacking weight high raises the center of gravity and makes rollovers more likely. Use blocking to keep cargo from sliding, and tiedowns to hold it down: at least one tiedown for every 10 feet of cargo, and never fewer than two. A strong header board protects you from cargo sliding forward in a sudden stop. Cover cargo so it can't blow or spill onto the road.
Check your cargo and securement within the first 50 miles, then every 3 hours or 150 miles, whichever comes first, and after every break.

title: Air brakes
summary: How air brakes work, the key pressure numbers, and how to check them.
body: Air brakes use compressed air to stop the vehicle. An engine-driven compressor pumps air into storage tanks. A governor stops the compressor at about 125 psi (cut-out) and starts it again around 100 psi (cut-in). A safety valve opens at about 150 psi if pressure gets too high.

There are three systems: service brakes for normal stopping, parking brakes, and emergency brakes. Spring brakes are held off by air pressure. If pressure falls to between 20 and 45 psi, the springs apply the brakes automatically. Before that, a low-pressure warning must come on before pressure drops below 60 psi. If it does, stop safely as soon as you can.

Air brakes have brake lag: air takes about half a second to reach the brakes, which adds about 32 feet of stopping distance at 55 mph. Water and oil collect in the tanks, so drain them daily if they don't drain automatically. In cold weather, water can freeze and block the brakes.

Learn the leakage test. With the engine off and brakes released, a single vehicle should lose less than 2 psi per minute (3 for a combination). With the pedal held down, less than 3 psi per minute (4 for a combination). Pressure should build from 85 to 100 psi within 45 seconds in a dual air system.

title: Combination vehicles and coupling
summary: Driving tractor-trailers safely, and how to couple and uncouple.
body: Combinations are harder to drive than single vehicles. Quick steering moves get amplified toward the back of the rig, the crack-the-whip effect, and can tip the trailer over even when the tractor stays upright. A loaded rig is far more likely to roll over than an empty one, so steer gently and slow down before curves.
In turns, trailer wheels follow a shorter path than the tractor's (off-tracking), so plan wide turns. If the trailer wheels lock and the trailer swings out, release the brakes to let them grip again.

Two air lines connect tractor and trailer. The red emergency (supply) line keeps the trailer tanks filled and controls its emergency brakes; if it breaks, the trailer brakes come on. The blue service line carries the air that applies the trailer brakes when you press the pedal. The tractor protection valve keeps air in the tractor if the trailer breaks away. The red eight-sided knob supplies air to the trailer; the yellow diamond knob is the parking brake.

To couple, chock the trailer or set its brakes, and set the trailer just low enough that it lifts slightly when you back under. Back until the fifth wheel touches, connect the air lines, then back under slowly until it locks. Check that there's no gap between the upper and lower fifth wheel and that the jaws are locked around the kingpin's shank. Do a tug test in low gear against the trailer brakes, then raise the landing gear fully.

title: Endorsements: hazmat, tanker, doubles, passenger and school bus
summary: What each endorsement covers and the key facts for each test.
body: Hazmat (H) requires a TSA background check and ELDT theory before the knowledge test. Placarded vehicles need placards on all four sides. Shipping papers go in the door pouch or within reach while you're belted in, and on the seat when you leave the cab. Placarded vehicles stop 15 to 50 feet from railroad tracks, and no smoking within 25 feet of the cargo.

Tank vehicles (N) are required for tanks of 119 gallons or more, or 1,000 gallons total. Liquid surge can push a truck forward or sideways. Baffles slow front-to-back surge but not side-to-side surge, and smooth-bore tanks have none. Leave outage for liquids to expand, and take curves well below the posted speed.

Doubles and triples (T): the last trailer is the most likely to roll over, so put the heaviest trailer up front. After coupling, open the shut-off valves on the front trailers and close the ones at the back of the last trailer.

Passenger (P): no riders may stand in front of the standee line, buses may carry no more than 500 pounds of allowed hazmat, and buses stop 15 to 50 feet from railroad crossings. School bus (S), which also needs P: the danger zone extends up to 30 feet around the bus, students cross about 10 feet in front where you can see them, and you count every student before pulling away.
